cards.q: What decides whether an element is in the s, p, d or f block?
cards.a: The sub-shell (s, p, d or f) that holds its highest-energy electron. This follows from its position in the Periodic Table, which is set by its proton number.
cards.why: Groups 1 and 2 are the s-block; Groups 13 to 18 the p-block; the transition elements the d-block; the lanthanides and actinides the f-block.

cards.q: State the block of each element: calcium, bromine, iron and uranium.
cards.a: Calcium: s. Bromine: p. Iron: d. Uranium: f.
cards.why: Ca ends \(\mathrm{4s^{2}}\); Br ends \(\mathrm{4p^{5}}\); Fe fills \(\mathrm{3d}\); U is an actinide, filling \(\mathrm{5f}\).

cards.q: Helium is placed in Group 18, above neon. Which block is it in, strictly, and why is it put there?
cards.a: Strictly the s-block: its configuration is \(\mathrm{1s^{2}}\). It is placed in Group 18 because, like the other noble gases, it has a full outer shell and is unreactive.
cards.why: Position in the table reflects chemical properties as well as the sub-shell being filled.

cards.q: What is meant by periodicity?
cards.a: A repeating pattern of physical and chemical properties across each period of the Periodic Table.
cards.why: It happens because the outer electron configuration repeats in each period: ns¹, ns², then ns²np¹ to ns²np⁶.

cards.q: Compare the outer electron configurations of Period 2 and Period 3 elements. How does this explain periodicity?
cards.a: Period 2 goes from \(\mathrm{2s^{1}}\) (Li) to \(\mathrm{2s^{2}2p^{6}}\) (Ne); Period 3 repeats this from \(\mathrm{3s^{1}}\) (Na) to \(\mathrm{3s^{2}3p^{6}}\) (Ar).
cards.why: Elements in the same group have the same outer configuration, so properties repeat from one period to the next.

cards.q: Explain why atomic radius decreases across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
cards.a: Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same.
marks: The number of protons (nuclear charge) increases across the period.
Electrons are added to the same (third) shell, so shielding is similar.
The outer electrons are attracted more strongly and pulled closer to the nucleus.

cards.q: True or false: atoms get bigger across a period because they have more electrons.
cards.a: False. They get smaller.
cards.why: The extra electrons go into the same shell, and the increasing nuclear charge pulls that shell in.

cards.q: Describe the pattern of first ionisation energies from sodium to argon.
cards.a: A general increase from Na to Ar, with small drops at aluminium (below Mg) and at sulfur (below P).
cards.why: Na is the lowest in the period; Ar the highest.

cards.q: Explain the general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3.
cards.a: Increasing nuclear charge, similar shielding, smaller atoms.
marks: Nuclear charge increases across the period.
The outer electron is in the same shell, so shielding is similar.
Atomic radius decreases, so the outer electron is attracted more strongly and more energy is needed to remove it.

cards.q: Explain the drops in first ionisation energy at aluminium and at sulfur in Period 3.
cards.a: Al: the electron removed is in a higher-energy 3p sub-shell. S: it is a paired 3p electron.
marks: Aluminium’s outer electron is in \(\mathrm{3p}\), which is higher in energy than magnesium’s \(\mathrm{3s}\).
The \(\mathrm{3p}\) electron is partly shielded by the \(\mathrm{3s}\) electrons, so it is easier to remove.
In sulfur, one \(\mathrm{3p}\) orbital holds a pair of electrons.
Repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove than phosphorus’s unpaired electrons.

cards.q: Which two elements in Period 2 show a drop in first ionisation energy, and why?
cards.a:
Boron (below Be): its outer electron is in \(\mathrm{2p}\), higher in energy than \(\mathrm{2s}\).
Oxygen (below N): it has a paired \(\mathrm{2p}\) electron that is repelled by its partner.
cards.why: The same pattern appears in Period 3 at Al and S: an example of periodicity.

cards.q: Describe the shape of a plot of first ionisation energy against atomic number for elements 1 to 20.
cards.a: A repeating pattern: a peak at each noble gas (He, Ne, Ar), a sharp fall to a minimum at each Group 1 metal (Li, Na, K), then a general rise across each period with small dips at Groups 13 and 16.
cards.why: Helium has the highest first ionisation energy of all; each new period starts with an electron in a new, further shell.

cards.q: First ionisation energies (\(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)): Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 787, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1521. Which features of these data illustrate periodicity?
cards.a: The general rise from Na to Ar, and the dips at Al and S, match the rise from Li to Ne with dips at B and O in Period 2.
cards.why: Each Period 3 value is lower than the Period 2 value for the same group: the outer electron is further from the nucleus.

cards.q: Give the structure and bonding of each element in Period 3, from sodium to argon.
cards.a:
Na, Mg, Al: giant metallic.
Si: giant covalent (macromolecular).
P₄, S₈, Cl₂: simple molecular.
Ar: monatomic.
cards.why: The structure decides what must be overcome on melting: metallic bonds, covalent bonds, or van der Waals forces.

cards.q: Describe the trend in melting point across Period 3.
cards.a: It rises from Na to Al, reaches a maximum at silicon, falls sharply to phosphorus, rises slightly to sulfur, then falls through chlorine to argon (the lowest).
cards.why: Silicon is highest and argon lowest; the big drop between Si and P marks the change from a giant structure to simple molecules.

cards.q: Explain why the melting point increases from sodium to magnesium to aluminium.
cards.a: Metallic bonding gets stronger.
marks: Each is a giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
From Na to Al, the ion charge increases (+1, +2, +3) and more electrons per atom are delocalised (1, 2, 3).
The ions also get smaller.
So the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger and more energy is needed to break it.

cards.q: Explain why silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3.
cards.a: It is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure.
marks: Silicon forms a giant covalent lattice, like diamond: each atom is bonded to four others.
Melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds.
This needs a large amount of energy.

cards.q: Explain the order of melting points of phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon: S > P > Cl > Ar.
cards.a: All are simple molecular (or atomic): melting overcomes van der Waals forces, which increase with the number of electrons.
marks: They exist as \(\mathrm{S_{8}}\), \(\mathrm{P_{4}}\), \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) molecules and Ar atoms.
Melting only overcomes van der Waals forces between molecules, not covalent bonds.
Larger molecules have more electrons, so stronger van der Waals forces: \(\mathrm{S_{8}} > \mathrm{P_{4}} > \mathrm{Cl_{2}} > \mathrm{Ar}\).

cards.q: True or false: when sulfur melts, the S–S covalent bonds break.
cards.a: False. Only the van der Waals forces between \(\mathrm{S_{8}}\) molecules are overcome.
cards.why: Breaking covalent bonds would need far more energy: that is why silicon, not sulfur, has a very high melting point.

cards.q: Describe and explain the pattern in melting points across Period 2 (Li to Ne).
cards.a: They rise from Li (metallic) through Be to a maximum at carbon (giant covalent, as diamond or graphite), then fall sharply to very low values for N₂, O₂, F₂ and Ne (simple molecular or atomic).
cards.why: The same shape as Period 3, with its maximum at silicon in the same group: periodicity.

cards.q: How do boiling temperatures across Period 3 compare with the melting temperatures?
cards.a: They follow the same overall pattern, with silicon highest and argon lowest. Aluminium boils far higher than sodium, as liquid metals still have strong metallic bonding to overcome.
cards.why: Boiling breaks all the remaining attractions between particles, so it reflects the bonding even more strongly than melting.

cards.q: Write the equation for sodium reacting with water, and give two observations.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2Na(s) + 2H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_{2}(g)}\)
Sodium floats, melts into a ball, fizzes and moves around until it disappears.
cards.why: The solution formed is strongly alkaline, about pH 14.

cards.q: Write equations for magnesium with cold water and with steam.
cards.a:
Cold water: \(\mathrm{Mg(s) + 2H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow Mg(OH)_{2}(aq) + H_{2}(g)}\)
Steam: \(\mathrm{Mg(s) + H_{2}O(g) \rightarrow MgO(s) + H_{2}(g)}\)
cards.why: With cold water the reaction is very slow and the solution only weakly alkaline (about pH 10); in steam magnesium burns with a bright white flame.

cards.q: Why does sodium react much more vigorously with water than magnesium does?
cards.a: Sodium loses one electron more easily than magnesium loses two.
cards.why: Sodium has a lower first ionisation energy, and magnesium must also lose a second electron, so sodium forms its ion more readily.

cards.q: Write equations for sodium, magnesium and aluminium burning in oxygen.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{4Na(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2Na_{2}O(s)}\)
\(\mathrm{2Mg(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2MgO(s)}\)
\(\mathrm{4Al(s) + 3O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2Al_{2}O_{3}(s)}\)
cards.why: Sodium burns with an orange-yellow flame; magnesium and aluminium with a brilliant white flame. All give white solids.

cards.q: Write equations for silicon, phosphorus and sulfur burning in oxygen.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Si(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow SiO_{2}(s)}\)
\(\mathrm{P_{4}(s) + 5O_{2}(g) \rightarrow P_{4}O_{10}(s)}\)
\(\mathrm{S(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow SO_{2}(g)}\)
cards.why: Phosphorus burns with a white flame giving white smoke; sulfur burns with a blue flame giving a choking gas.

cards.q: How is \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) made from \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\)? Write the equation.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_{3}(g)}\), with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\).
cards.why: Burning sulfur in air gives mainly SO₂; further oxidation is slow without a catalyst.

cards.q: What is the oxidation state of the Period 3 element in \(\mathrm{Na_{2}O}\), \(\mathrm{MgO}\), \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\)?
cards.why: In these highest oxides, the oxidation state equals the number of outer-shell electrons, so it rises by one each group.

cards.q: Classify the structure and bonding in each oxide: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃ and SO₂.
cards.a:
Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃: giant ionic.
SiO₂: giant covalent (macromolecular).
P₄O₁₀, SO₃, SO₂: simple molecular.
cards.why: Bonding changes from ionic to covalent across the period as the electronegativity difference with oxygen decreases.

cards.q: Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium oxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a higher charge and is smaller than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\).
marks: Both are giant ionic lattices held by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a greater charge (and smaller radius) than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\).
So the attraction between \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) is stronger, and more energy is needed to break the lattice.

cards.q: Explain why aluminium oxide has a lower melting point than magnesium oxide, even though Al³⁺ has a greater charge.
cards.a: The ionic bonding in aluminium oxide has some covalent character.
marks: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) is small and highly charged, so it polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) ion.
This gives the bonding partial covalent character.
The lattice is weakened compared with a purely ionic one, so less energy is needed to melt it.

cards.q: Explain why silicon dioxide has a high melting point but phosphorus(V) oxide and sulfur trioxide have low melting points.
cards.a: SiO₂ is giant covalent; P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ are simple molecular.
marks: SiO₂ is a giant covalent (macromolecular) lattice; melting breaks many strong covalent bonds.
\(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) are simple molecules; melting only overcomes weak van der Waals forces between molecules.
\(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) melts higher than \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) because its larger molecules have stronger van der Waals forces.

cards.q: Describe the trend in melting point of the highest oxides from Na₂O to SO₃.
cards.a: High for the ionic oxides, with MgO highest; still high for SiO₂ (giant covalent); then much lower for P₄O₁₀ and lowest for SO₃ (simple molecular).
cards.why: Order: MgO > Al₂O₃ > SiO₂ > Na₂O ≫ P₄O₁₀ > SO₃.

cards.q: Write equations for sodium oxide and magnesium oxide reacting with water, and give the approximate pH of each solution.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Na_{2}O(s) + H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq)}\): pH about 14.
\(\mathrm{MgO(s) + H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow Mg(OH)_{2}(aq)}\): pH about 9.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) is only slightly soluble, so fewer \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions are released and the solution is less alkaline.

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for sodium oxide dissolving in water.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Na_{2}O(s) + H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow 2Na^{+}(aq) + 2OH^{-}(aq)}\)
cards.why: The oxide ion is a strong base: \(\mathrm{O^{2-} + H_{2}O \rightarrow 2OH^{-}}\).

cards.q: What happens when aluminium oxide and silicon dioxide are added to water? What is the pH?
cards.a: Neither reacts or dissolves, so the water stays at pH 7.
cards.why: Al₂O₃ has a very strong ionic lattice and SiO₂ a giant covalent structure; neither is broken up by water.

cards.q: Write equations for phosphorus(V) oxide, sulfur dioxide and sulfur trioxide reacting with water. Give the approximate pH of each solution.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10} + 6H_{2}O \rightarrow 4H_{3}PO_{4}}\): pH about 0–1.
\(\mathrm{SO_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{3}}\): pH about 2–3.
\(\mathrm{SO_{3} + H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{4}}\): pH about 0.
cards.why: Sulfurous acid is a weak acid, so its solution is less acidic than sulfuric or phosphoric acid of similar concentration.

cards.q: Write equations showing the ions formed when sulfur dioxide and sulfur trioxide dissolve in water.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{SO_{2} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + HSO_{3}^{-}}\)
\(\mathrm{SO_{3} + H_{2}O \rightarrow 2H^{+} + SO_{4}^{2-}}\)
cards.why: Sulfurous acid is weak, so the first is an equilibrium lying to the left; sulfuric acid is strong.

cards.q: Explain how the type of bonding in the Period 3 oxides relates to the pH of the solutions they form with water.
cards.a: Ionic oxides are basic; covalent oxides are acidic.
marks: Ionic oxides (\(\mathrm{Na_{2}O}\), \(\mathrm{MgO}\)) contain \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) ions, which accept protons from water to form \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\): alkaline solutions.
Simple covalent oxides (\(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\), \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\)) react with water to form acids, which release \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\): acidic solutions.
\(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\) are insoluble, so the pH stays at 7.

cards.q: Describe the structure of phosphoric(V) acid, \(\mathrm{H_{3}PO_{4}}\), and of the phosphate ion it forms.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{H_{3}PO_{4}}\): a central P atom with one P=O double bond and three P–O–H groups, arranged tetrahedrally.
\(\mathrm{PO_{4}^{3-}}\): all three H atoms lost as \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\); a tetrahedral ion with the 3− charge spread over the O atoms.
cards.why: The acidic hydrogens are the ones bonded to oxygen, in O–H groups.

cards.q: Describe the structures of sulfuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\), and of the sulfate ion.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\): a central S atom with two S=O double bonds and two S–O–H groups, arranged tetrahedrally.
\(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\): both H lost; a tetrahedral ion with the 2− charge spread over the O atoms.
cards.why: It can lose one proton to form \(\mathrm{HSO_{4}^{-}}\), or both to form \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\).

cards.q: Describe the structures of sulfurous acid, \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{3}}\), and of the sulfite ion.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{3}}\): a central S atom with one S=O double bond, two S–O–H groups and a lone pair (trigonal pyramidal).
\(\mathrm{SO_{3}^{2-}}\): both H lost; a trigonal pyramidal ion with a lone pair on S.
cards.why: Sulfur is +4 here, not +6, so it keeps a lone pair.

cards.q: Write equations for sodium oxide and magnesium oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Na_{2}O + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_{2}O}\)
\(\mathrm{MgO + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_{2} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Basic oxides react with acids to form a salt and water.

cards.q: What is an amphoteric oxide? Which Period 3 oxide is amphoteric?
cards.a: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases. Aluminium oxide, \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}\).
cards.why: Its bonding is ionic with significant covalent character, between the basic ionic oxides and the acidic covalent ones.

cards.q: Write equations for aluminium oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid and with sulfuric acid.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3} + 6HCl \rightarrow 2AlCl_{3} + 3H_{2}O}\)
\(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3} + 3H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow Al_{2}(SO_{4})_{3} + 3H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Acting as a base, aluminium oxide forms an aluminium salt and water.

cards.q: Write the equation for aluminium oxide dissolving in sodium hydroxide solution.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3} + 2NaOH + 3H_{2}O \rightarrow 2NaAl(OH)_{4}}\)
cards.why: Acting as an acid, it forms the tetrahydroxoaluminate ion, \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_{4}^{-}}\). Ionic: \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3} + 2OH^{-} + 3H_{2}O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_{4}^{-}}\).

cards.q: Silicon dioxide does not dissolve in water. How can you show it is an acidic oxide? Write the equation.
cards.a: It reacts with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide: \(\mathrm{SiO_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}SiO_{3} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: It also reacts with basic oxides, e.g. \(\mathrm{SiO_{2} + CaO \rightarrow CaSiO_{3}}\), which removes sand impurities in the blast furnace.

cards.q: Write the equation for phosphorus(V) oxide reacting with excess sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10} + 12NaOH \rightarrow 4Na_{3}PO_{4} + 6H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Check: 12 Na, 12 H and 22 O on each side. Phosphoric acid itself reacts as \(\mathrm{H_{3}PO_{4} + 3NaOH \rightarrow Na_{3}PO_{4} + 3H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: Write equations for sulfur dioxide and sulfur trioxide reacting with sodium hydroxide.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{SO_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}SO_{3} + H_{2}O}\)
\(\mathrm{SO_{3} + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}SO_{4} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Acidic oxides react with bases to form a salt (sodium sulfite or sodium sulfate) and water.

cards.q: True or false: silicon dioxide is a neutral oxide because it gives pH 7 when added to water.
cards.a: False. It is an acidic oxide.
cards.why: It gives pH 7 only because it is insoluble; it reacts with bases such as hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide to form a salt.

cards.q: Summarise the acid–base character of the oxides across Period 3, from Na₂O to SO₃.
cards.a: Basic (Na₂O, MgO) → amphoteric (Al₂O₃) → acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃).
cards.why: This follows the change from ionic to covalent bonding across the period.
